chapters.title: Chapter 2: The One-Step and Multi-Step Binomial Tree

lessons.title: Replicating Portfolios: Why the Binomial Price Must Be Arbitrage-Free

children.text: Lesson 1 handed over a formula, f equals the discounted, risk-neutral expected payoff, and asked you to trust it. This lesson does not ask for trust. It builds the replicating portfolio explicitly, in the same u, d, r notation, and shows exactly what happens to anyone foolish enough to trade the option away from that price. The binomial price is not a reasonable estimate, it is the unique price that closes off every riskless profit.

The replicating portfolio holds Delta shares of the stock and B rupees in the risk-free asset, B negative meaning borrowed. Delta is chosen so the portfolio's value matches the derivative's payoff in both the up and down states.

body.caption: The number of shares that makes the portfolio move exactly like the derivative, one step at a time.
The risk-free position, borrowed if negative, that makes the up-state equation balance exactly. The down-state equation balances automatically once Delta and B are set this way.

body.text: The portfolio's cost today, Delta times S0 plus B, is not a separate number from Lesson 1's f = e^(−r delta-t) [p fu + (1 − p) fd]. Expand both formulas algebraically and they collapse into the exact same expression. Two routes, replicate the payoff directly, or discount under risk-neutral probability, landing on an identical price is not a coincidence, it is what no-arbitrage guarantees.

children.text: What Happens If the Market Disagrees

The replicating portfolio and the derivative produce the identical payoff in every possible future state, there is no third outcome. Two things with identical payoffs in every state must trade at the same price today, otherwise anyone can buy the cheap one, sell the expensive one, and bank the difference risk-free, with the future payoffs cancelling out exactly. If the option trades above f, sell it and buy the replicating portfolio. If it trades below f, buy it and sell the replicating portfolio short. Either direction locks in the gap as pure profit, with zero net exposure to whether the stock actually goes up or down.
Worked Example: Trading Against a Mispriced Option

Reuse Lesson 1's exact setup, S0 = ₹100, u = 1.2, d = 0.9, r = 5% continuous, a ₹100-strike call, fair value f = ₹9.59, Delta = 0.6667, B = −₹57.07. Suppose a system error on some exchange lists this call at ₹11. Here is the trade that exploits it, and its full cash flow across today, the up state, and the down state.

body.caption: The arbitrage trade against a call mispriced at ₹11 (fair value ₹9.59)

body.text: Read the Net row carefully. Whatever the stock does, rises to ₹120 or falls to ₹90, the up-state and down-state columns net to exactly zero, the shares and the loan repayment always cover the call obligation precisely. The only nonzero number in the whole table is the ₹1.41 pocketed today, and it does not depend on the stock's outcome at all. That is the textbook definition of an arbitrage, riskless profit with no capital ultimately at stake.

children.text: The underpriced direction mirrors this exactly. If the same call traded at ₹8 instead, buying the call and selling the replicating portfolio short, sell 0.6667 shares, lend the proceeds, locks in the ₹1.59 gap between ₹9.59 and ₹8 just as risklessly, with the same zero net exposure at expiry.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: The same call from the worked example is mispriced at ₹8 instead of its fair value of ₹9.59. Which trade locks in a riskless profit?
options: Write the call and buy the replicating portfolio
Buy the call and sell the replicating portfolio short
Do nothing, since an underpriced option carries no arbitrage
Buy the call and hold it to expiry with no hedge
body.explanation: An underpriced option is the mirror image of an overpriced one. Buying the cheap call and shorting the exact replicating portfolio that reproduces its payoff locks in the ₹1.59 gap today, with the short portfolio's payoff exactly cancelling the call's payoff in both the up and down states at expiry.

body.title: Does This Matter With Real Transaction Costs?
body.scenario: A student points out that real NSE trading involves bid-ask spreads, brokerage, and margin requirements, none of which appeared in the arbitrage table above, and asks whether the whole no-arbitrage argument is therefore just a theoretical exercise.
body.modelAnswer: Real frictions don't erase the argument, they turn a single exact price into a narrow no-arbitrage band around it, small enough that trading against a mispricing inside that band would cost more in spreads and margin than it earns. What the frictions don't remove is the anchor itself, market makers and prop desks still quote around the theoretical price, because any mispricing large enough to clear transaction costs attracts exactly the kind of arbitrage trade built above, competed away quickly by whoever spots it first. That competitive pressure is precisely why liquid Nifty and Bank Nifty option prices track model prices as closely as they do in practice, not because the model is a legal requirement, but because deviating from it leaves money on the table for someone else to take.

body.text: The binomial price is not a reasonable estimate. It is the unique price that leaves no way to build a portfolio that earns a certain profit. Every rupee above or below it is a guaranteed payday sitting on the table for whoever builds the replicating portfolio first.

points: The replicating portfolio, Delta shares plus a risk-free position B, is built to match the derivative's payoff exactly in both the up and down states.
Its cost today, Delta times S0 plus B, is algebraically identical to Lesson 1's risk-neutral formula, two different-looking routes to the exact same number.

If the option trades above fair value, write it and buy the replica. If it trades below, buy it and sell the replica short. Either way, the future payoffs cancel exactly and the price gap is banked risklessly today.
The worked example showed this with real numbers: a call mispriced at ₹11 against a ₹9.59 fair value produces a guaranteed ₹1.41 today and exactly ₹0 in both future states.

Real-world frictions turn the exact price into a narrow no-arbitrage band rather than eliminating the logic, and competitive arbitrage trading is exactly why real option prices stay close to model prices.
